questions.q: What should drive the design of a dangerous-capability evaluation, according to this lesson?
options: Whatever benchmark is most convenient to run
A concrete threat model — a specific story about how the capability could cause real-world harm
The model's marketing specifications
The amount of compute available for training, not evaluation
questions.explain: Starting from a specific threat model ensures the evaluation measures the actual risk rather than something merely adjacent to it.

questions.q: Why does a threat model need to be turned into a task suite with objective, checkable criteria?
options: So that a human or automated checker can determine pass or fail without ambiguity
Because objective criteria are required by law in every jurisdiction
Because task suites are faster to compute than any other format
So that the model being tested can grade its own performance
questions.explain: A vague prompt and a gut-feel judgment don't produce a trustworthy, repeatable measurement — discrete, scorable tasks do.

questions.q: Why do dangerous-capability evaluations deliberately push elicitation as hard as possible (fine-tuning, scaffolding, jailbreak techniques)?
options: To make the model perform as poorly as possible on purpose
To find the model's true capability ceiling rather than its resting-state behavior, since a real attacker would push just as hard
Because gentler testing is against industry regulation
Because elicitation has no effect on evaluation results
questions.explain: Under-eliciting produces a false sense of safety, since a real attacker with resources and motivation would not stop at a gentle prompt.

questions.q: Why does a raw capability-eval score mean little without a human-expert baseline?
options: Because raw scores are always fabricated by the lab running the test
Because what matters is uplift relative to what a resourced human attacker could already achieve with existing tools and public information
Because human baselines are purely symbolic and not actually measured
Because capability evaluations never produce numeric scores
questions.explain: A high raw score may not represent new marginal risk if a human could already achieve similar results without the model, which is why uplift over baseline is the meaningful comparison.

questions.q: What is the practical consequence of under-eliciting a model during a dangerous-capability evaluation?
options: It has no consequence since elicitation doesn't affect eval outcomes
It produces a false sense of safety that can be worse than not testing at all, because it looks like evidence of safety
It always causes the evaluation to overestimate risk
It guarantees the model will pass every safety evaluation as well
questions.explain: A gentle evaluation that fails to surface a real capability can be mistaken for genuine evidence that the capability isn't present, which is more dangerous than an honest gap in testing.
